Actual Article Body:
‘Bizarrely, you have chalked your motives up to nothing more than “gay” “pettiness” rather than any legislative purpose and compared yourself to a demonic clown,’ Scharf told Garcia.

In response to the White House warning Congress that malicious investigations are unconstitutional, The New York Times claims that threats to prosecute executive branch staff are of no concern, but the executive checking the power of Congress is a national scandal.

The New York Times published a piece Wednesday titled “White House Threatens Congress, Saying Aggressive Investigations Could Be Crime.” It detailed a letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf to incoming House Oversight Committee Chairman Robert Garcia, D-Calif., wherein Garcia is informed of the constitutional limits on what he and the rest of the Democrats appear to have planned for the next Congress: a barrage of subpoenas and investigations with the “clear intent to transgress” on a coequal branch.

“The Supreme Court has held that ‘[i]nvestigations conducted solely for the personal aggrandizement of the investigators or to ‘punish’ those investigated are indefensible.’ Congressional investigations must further a legitimate legislative task; Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary,” Scharf’s letter stated. “These principles require Congress to identify a legitimate legislative purpose underlying its investigative acts. Failure to do so in this context represents a clear abuse of power and an affront to our constitutional system of government and to the rule of law.”

On the night of the midterm elections, Garcia ominously wrote “LAWYER UP,” with many other Democrats following suit in threatening political persecution and prosecution of any staff associated with the Trump administration. Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., infamously threatened to destroy the lives of young conservatives who want to work in the administration, and it appears those threats may soon become reality.

Scharf’s letter stated that such conduct “may cross the line into blatant criminality. And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation.”
